p.src: Now Mi Fang, hearing that Jingzhou had fallen, was at a loss what to do. Suddenly it was reported that Fu Shiren, the commander defending Gong'an, had arrived. Mi Fang hurriedly admitted him into the city and asked what had happened. Fu Shiren said, “It is not that I was disloyal; the situation was perilous and my strength exhausted, so I could hold out no longer. I have now surrendered to Eastern Wu; you too would do better to surrender without delay.” Mi Fang said, “We have received great kindness from the King of Hanzhong. How could we bear to betray him?” Fu Shiren said, “When Lord Guan departed, he bitterly resented the two of us. If he returns victorious one day, he will certainly not pardon us lightly. Consider it carefully.” Mi Fang said, “My brother and I have long served the King of Hanzhong. How could we turn against him overnight?” While he was still wavering, it was suddenly reported that Lord Guan had sent an envoy, who was admitted into the hall. The envoy said, “Lord Guan's army lacks provisions. I have come expressly to collect one hundred thousand shi of white rice from Nan Commandery and Gong'an. The two generals are ordered to escort it through the night and deliver it at the front. Any delay will be punished by immediate execution.” Mi Fang was greatly alarmed and turned to Fu Shiren, saying, “Now that Jingzhou has been taken by Eastern Wu, how can these provisions possibly get through?” Fu Shiren cried sternly, “There is no need for further hesitation!” He drew his sword and struck down the envoy there in the hall. Mi Fang exclaimed in alarm, “What have you done?” Fu Shiren said, “Lord Guan's intention is precisely to have the two of us killed. How can we bind our hands and await death? If you do not surrender to Eastern Wu now, Lord Guan will surely kill you.” As they spoke, it was suddenly reported that Lü Meng was leading troops in an assault upon the city walls. Mi Fang was greatly alarmed and went out of the city with Fu Shiren to surrender. Lü Meng was delighted and presented them to Sun Quan. Sun Quan rewarded them both handsomely. Once the people had been pacified, he lavishly feasted the entire army.

p.src: At this time Cao Cao was in the capital Xu, discussing the affairs of Jingzhou with his advisers, when it was suddenly reported that Eastern Wu had sent an envoy bearing a letter. Cao Cao summoned him inside, and the envoy presented the letter. Cao Cao opened and read it. The letter explained in detail that Wu's forces were about to raid Jingzhou and asked Cao Cao to attack Yun Chang from the other side; it also urged him not to divulge the matter, lest Yun Chang be put on his guard. Cao Cao discussed the matter with his advisers. Dong Zhao, the chief secretary, said, “Fancheng is now under siege, craning its neck in hope of rescue. We should have someone shoot the letter into the city to reassure the troops; and we should also let Lord Guan learn that Eastern Wu is about to raid Jingzhou. Fearing the loss of Jingzhou, he will surely withdraw in haste; then Xu Huang can seize the opportunity to fall upon him, and we shall win complete success.” Cao Cao followed his plan, on the one hand sending a man to urge Xu Huang to attack at once; on the other, he personally led a great army to Yanglingpo, south of Luoyang, and encamped there to relieve Cao Ren.

p.src: Now Xu Huang was seated in his tent when it was suddenly reported that an envoy from the King of Wei had arrived. Xu Huang admitted him and questioned him. The envoy said, “The King of Wei is now leading his army and has already passed Luoyang. He commands you to engage Lord Guan without delay and lift the siege of Fancheng.” While he was speaking, a scout reported, “Guan Ping has stationed troops at Yancheng, and Liao Hua at Sizhong. There are twelve fortified camps from front to rear, linked in an unbroken chain.” Xu Huang immediately sent his deputies Xu Shang and Lü Jian, displaying Xu Huang's banners as a ruse, to Yancheng to engage Guan Ping. Xu Huang himself led five hundred picked troops along the Mian River to strike at Yancheng from the rear.

p.src: Now when Guan Ping heard that Xu Huang himself was leading troops against him, he took his own forces out to meet the enemy. The two armies drew up facing each other. Guan Ping rode forth and crossed weapons with Xu Shang; after only three bouts, Xu Shang was soundly defeated and fled. Lü Jian came out to fight but was likewise defeated after five or six bouts and fled. Guan Ping pursued them for more than twenty li, pressing his victory, when it was suddenly reported that fire had broken out in the city. Realizing that he had fallen into a trap, Guan Ping hastily wheeled his troops around to save Yancheng, only to encounter a formidable force drawn up before him. Xu Huang sat mounted beneath his command banner and shouted, “My worthy nephew Guan Ping, how utterly heedless you are of death! Your Jingzhou has already been seized by Eastern Wu, yet you still run rampant here!” Guan Ping was enraged. Spurring his horse and brandishing his blade, he charged straight at Xu Huang. Before three or four bouts had passed, the troops raised a great cry, and flames surged high within Yancheng. Guan Ping dared not prolong the fight. He hacked open a path and made straight for the camp at Sizhong. Liao Hua came out to receive him. Liao Hua said, “Men say that Jingzhou has already been raided by Lü Meng. The army is in a panic—what are we to do?” Guan Ping said, “That must be a false rumor. Any soldier who repeats it shall be beheaded.”

p.src: Suddenly an express rider arrived, reporting that the first encampment due north was under attack by troops led by Xu Huang. Guan Ping said, “If the first encampment is lost, how can any of the other camps remain secure? This place is protected by the Mian River, so the enemy will not dare come here. You and I shall go together to relieve the first encampment.” Liao Hua summoned a subordinate commander and instructed him, “You must hold this camp firmly. If the enemy comes, light the signal fires at once.” The subordinate said, “The camp at Sizhong has ten ranks of chevaux-de-frise; not even a bird could fly in. Why should we fear enemy troops?” Guan Ping and Liao Hua then raised all the picked troops from the camp at Sizhong and hurried to garrison the first encampment. Seeing the Wei troops encamped on a low hill, Guan Ping said to Liao Hua, “Xu Huang has chosen unfavorable ground for his camp. Tonight we can lead our troops in a raid upon it.” Liao Hua said, “General, take half the troops with you. I shall guard this camp carefully.”

p.src: That night Guan Ping led a force into the Wei camp, but found not a soul there. Realizing it was a trap, Guan Ping was hastily withdrawing when Xu Shang attacked from the left and Lü Jian from the right, assailing him from both sides. Guan Ping suffered a crushing defeat and returned to camp. The Wei troops pursued their advantage and surrounded it on all sides. Unable to hold out, Guan Ping and Liao Hua abandoned the first encampment and made straight for the camp at Sizhong. From afar they could already see flames rising within the camp. They hurried to the camp, only to see Wei banners everywhere. Guan Ping and the others withdrew and hastened away along the main road to Fancheng. An army blocked the way ahead, led by none other than the great general Xu Huang. Guan Ping and Liao Hua fought desperately, forced open a path, and escaped. Returning to the main camp, they went before Lord Guan and said, “Xu Huang has now seized Yancheng and the surrounding positions; moreover, Cao Cao himself is leading a great army in three divisions to relieve Fancheng; and many are saying that Jingzhou has already been raided by Lü Meng.” Lord Guan shouted, “That is merely a false rumor spread by the enemy to unsettle my army! Lü Meng of Eastern Wu is gravely ill, and the mere youngster Lu Xun has replaced him. There is nothing to fear!”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, it was suddenly reported that Xu Huang's troops had arrived, and Lord Guan ordered his horse prepared. Guan Ping remonstrated, “Father, your body has not yet fully recovered. You must not face the enemy.” Lord Guan said, “Xu Huang is an old acquaintance of mine, and I know his abilities well. If he will not withdraw, I shall behead him first as a warning to the other Wei generals.” He donned his armor, took up his blade, mounted his horse, and rode forth in high spirits. At the sight of him, every man in the Wei army was struck with fear. Lord Guan reined in his horse and called, “Where is Xu Gongming?” The gate banners of the Wei camp parted, and Xu Huang rode out. Bowing slightly in the saddle, he said, “Since I parted from you, my lord, several years have passed in the blink of an eye. I never imagined that your beard and hair would already have turned gray. I recall how I attended you in the prime of life and received much instruction from you; I remain grateful and have never forgotten it. Now your heroic renown shakes all the realm of Huaxia; hearing of it, I, your old friend, cannot but admire and acclaim you! How fortunate that I may see you today; it deeply consoles my long-felt yearning.” Lord Guan said, “Gongming and I share a deep bond, unlike my relations with other men. Why, then, have you repeatedly driven my son into such straits?” Xu Huang turned to his generals and cried sternly, “Whoever takes Yun Chang's head shall be richly rewarded with a thousand pieces of gold!” Lord Guan exclaimed in surprise, “Gongming, why do you say such a thing?” Xu Huang replied, “Today this is an affair of the state. I dare not sacrifice public duty for private feeling.”

p.src: With that, he swung his great axe and charged straight at Lord Guan. Lord Guan, enraged, likewise brandished his blade and met him; they fought for more than eighty bouts. Though Lord Guan's martial skill was peerless, his right arm was still lacking in strength. Fearing harm might befall him, Guan Ping urgently sounded the gong for retreat. Lord Guan wheeled his horse back toward camp, when suddenly tremendous battle cries rose on every side. Cao Ren in Fan Castle, having heard that Cao Cao's relief force had arrived, had led his troops out of the city and joined Xu Huang, so that they attacked from both sides. The Jingzhou troops fell into chaos. Lord Guan mounted and led his officers in a hurried flight toward the upper reaches of the Xiang River. The Wei troops came pursuing from behind. Lord Guan hastily crossed the Xiang River and fled toward Xiangyang. Suddenly an express rider arrived, reporting, “Jingzhou has been seized by Lü Meng, and our families have fallen into his hands.” Lord Guan was greatly alarmed. Not daring to continue toward Xiangyang, he turned his army toward Gong'an. Another scout reported, “Fu Shiren of Gong'an has surrendered to Eastern Wu.” Lord Guan flew into a rage. Just then a grain-transport officer arrived and reported, “Fu Shiren of Gong'an went to Nanjun, killed the envoy, and induced Mi Fang to surrender with him to Eastern Wu.”

p.src: At these words, Lord Guan's fury choked him; his wound burst open, and he fell senseless to the ground. His officers revived him. Lord Guan turned to his military secretary Wang Fu and said, “I regret that I did not heed your counsel. Today this calamity has indeed come to pass!” Then he asked, “Why were no signal fires raised along the river, either upstream or downstream?” A scout replied, “Lü Meng had his sailors dress entirely in white and pose as merchants crossing the river, with elite troops concealed inside ||. They first captured the soldiers guarding the beacon towers, so no fires could be raised.” Lord Guan stamped his foot and sighed, “I have fallen into the traitor's scheme! How can I face my elder brother now?” Zhao Lei, the controller of provisions, said, “The situation is desperate. We should send a man to Chengdu to seek aid, while advancing overland to retake Jingzhou.” Lord Guan followed his advice, ordering Ma Liang and Yi Ji to carry three dispatches and ride through the night to Chengdu for aid; meanwhile, he led his troops to recover Jingzhou; he personally commanded the vanguard, leaving Liao Hua and Guan Ping to guard the rear.

p.src: Now that the siege of Fan Castle had been lifted, Cao Ren led his officers before Cao Cao, where he wept, bowed, and begged forgiveness. Cao Cao said, “This was ordained by Heaven; it was no fault of yours.” Cao Cao richly rewarded the entire army, then personally visited the camp at Sizhong and inspected its surroundings. Turning to his commanders, he said, “The Jingzhou troops had laid several rings of trenches and chevaux-de-frise, yet Xu Gongming penetrated deep within them and achieved complete victory. In more than thirty years of commanding armies, even I have never dared drive straight into an enemy encirclement. Gongming is truly a man of both courage and discernment!” All present exclaimed in admiration. Cao Cao withdrew his army and encamped at Mobei. When Xu Huang's troops arrived, Cao Cao personally came out of camp to welcome him. He saw that Xu Huang's men marched in perfect formation, without the least disorder. Cao Cao rejoiced and said, “General Xu truly has the bearing of Zhou Yafu!” He thereupon appointed Xu Huang General Who Pacifies the South and ordered him to defend Xiangyang with Xiahou Shang, so as to hold Lord Guan's army in check. As Jingzhou was not yet settled, Cao Cao kept his forces stationed at Mobei to await further news.

I am trapped between them, and our reinforcements have not come. What are we to do?” Zhao Lei said, “When Lü Meng was formerly at Lukou, he wrote to Your Lordship, and our two houses pledged friendship and agreed to destroy the traitor Cao together; yet now he has aided Cao and attacked us. This is a betrayal of the alliance. Your Lordship should station the army here for the moment and send Lü Meng a letter condemning him. Let us see how he replies.” Lord Guan followed his counsel, composed a letter, and dispatched an envoy to Jingzhou.

p.src: Meanwhile, in Jingzhou, Lü Meng issued an order: Wu soldiers were forbidden to disturb the households in any Jingzhou commandery whose men had gone to war with Lord Guan, and those households were to receive monthly rations of grain; where anyone was ill, a physician was sent to treat them. Grateful for his kindness, the soldiers' families remained peacefully in their homes. When word suddenly came that Lord Guan's envoy had arrived, Lü Meng went beyond the walls to welcome him, escorted him into the city, and treated him with the courtesies due a guest. The envoy presented the letter to Lü Meng. After reading it, Lü Meng said to the envoy, “The friendship I formerly formed with General Guan was merely my own private resolve; today's affair was commanded by my lord, and I had no power to decide for myself. I trouble you to report this to the general and convey my respectful regards.” He then gave a banquet for the envoy and sent him to rest at the posthouse. Thereupon the families of the soldiers who had gone on campaign all came to ask for news. Some entrusted him with letters, while others gave him oral messages; all said that their households were safe and lacked neither clothing nor food. The envoy took leave of Lü Meng, who personally escorted him out of the city. Returning to Lord Guan, the envoy reported Lü Meng's words in full, adding that within Jingzhou, Your Lordship's honored family and the families of all the officers were safe and lacked nothing in their provisions. Lord Guan raged, “This is the traitor's scheme! If I cannot slay this villain while alive, I shall surely slay him after death and avenge my hatred!” He shouted at the envoy to withdraw. When the envoy left the camp, the officers all came to ask about their families. The envoy told them in detail that every household was well and that Lü Meng had treated them with the utmost kindness; he also delivered the letters to the respective officers. The officers were delighted, and none retained any will to fight.

p.src: Lord Guan led his army toward Jingzhou, but as they marched, many soldiers deserted and returned there. Lord Guan's hatred and anger only grew, and he pressed the army onward. p.src: By the time they had fought until dusk, Lord Guan looked toward the surrounding hills and saw them filled with Jingzhou soldiers, calling for elder and younger brothers, seeking sons and fathers, their cries never ceasing. The hearts of his men wholly changed, and they all departed in answer to those calls. Lord Guan shouted for them to stop, but could not restrain them. Only a little over three hundred followers remained. They fought until the third watch, when battle cries shook the eastern sky: Guan Ping and Liao Hua had divided their troops into two columns and broken into the encirclement, rescuing Lord Guan. Guan Ping reported, “The army's morale is in ruins. We must secure a city in which to station ourselves temporarily while awaiting reinforcements. Though Maicheng is small, it will suffice for an encampment.” Lord Guan accepted the advice and hurried the remnants of his army to Maicheng. He divided his troops to guard all four gates closely, then assembled his officers for counsel. Zhao Lei said, “Shangyong is near here, and Liu Feng and Meng Da are presently stationed there. p.src: While they were deliberating, a sudden report came that the Wu forces had arrived and completely surrounded the city. Lord Guan asked, “Who dares break through the encirclement and go to Shangyong for aid?” Liao Hua said, “I am willing to go.” Guan Ping said, “I will escort you through the enemy lines.” Lord Guan at once wrote a letter and gave it to Liao Hua to conceal upon his person; after eating his fill, Liao Hua mounted his horse, and they opened the gate and left the city. They encountered the Wu general Ding Feng blocking their path, but Guan Ping charged and fought with all his might. Ding Feng was defeated and fled. Taking advantage of the moment, Liao Hua fought his way through the encirclement and headed for Shangyong. Guan Ping returned to the city and held it fast, refusing to come out.

p.src: Now Liu Feng and Meng Da had taken Shangyong, whereupon its governor, Shen Dan, led his people in surrender. The King of Hanzhong therefore appointed Liu Feng Deputy General and charged him to guard Shangyong together with Meng Da. That day, having learned of Lord Guan’s defeat, the two were in consultation when word suddenly came that Liao Hua had arrived. Liu Feng ordered that he be admitted and questioned him. Liao Hua said, “Lord Guan has been defeated and is now trapped in Maicheng, hard pressed by the siege. Reinforcements from Shu cannot arrive within a day or two. He therefore ordered me to break through the enemy lines and come here to seek aid. I beg you two generals to raise the troops of Shangyong at once and rescue him from this peril. If there is the least delay, Lord Guan will surely be lost.” Liu Feng said, “Rest for the moment, General, and allow me to deliberate.”

p.src: Liao Hua went to rest at the posthouse and waited solely for the troops to be dispatched. Liu Feng said to Meng Da, “My uncle is trapped. What are we to do?” Meng Da replied, “The troops of Eastern Wu are elite and their generals valiant. Moreover, all nine commanderies of Jingzhou now belong to them; only Maicheng remains, and that is but a tiny place. I have also heard that Cao Cao personally commands an army of four or five hundred thousand encamped at Mobei. How could the forces of our mountain stronghold possibly withstand the mighty armies of both powers? We must not rashly engage the enemy.” Liu Feng said, “I know that too. But Lord Guan is my uncle. How can I bear to sit by and watch without rescuing him?” Meng Da laughed and said, “You regard Lord Guan as your uncle, General, but I fear he may not regard you as his nephew. I heard that when the King of Hanzhong first adopted you as his heir, Lord Guan was displeased at once. Later, after the King of Hanzhong ascended his throne, he wished to appoint an heir and consulted Kongming. Kongming said, ‘This is a family matter; you need only ask Guan and Zhang.’ The King of Hanzhong therefore sent a man to Jingzhou to ask Lord Guan. Lord Guan said that you were merely an adopted son and must not presumptuously be made heir; he advised the King of Hanzhong to send you far away to the mountain stronghold of Shangyong, thereby averting future trouble. Everyone knows this. Can it be that you alone do not, General? Why, then, do you still pride yourself today upon the bond of uncle and nephew and wish to take reckless action at such risk?” Liu Feng said, “What you say is true, but on what grounds shall we refuse him?” Meng Da replied, “Simply say that the mountain city has only just submitted and the people’s allegiance is not yet settled, so we dare not hastily raise troops lest we lose the place entrusted to our defense.” Liu Feng followed his advice. The next day he summoned Liao Hua and said, “This mountain city has only recently submitted, so we cannot spare troops to aid you.” Liao Hua was aghast. Knocking his head upon the ground, he cried, “If that is so, Lord Guan is finished!” Meng Da said, “Even if we went now, how could a cup of water extinguish a cartload of burning firewood? You should return at once, General, and quietly await the arrival of the troops from Shu.” Liao Hua pleaded with them in bitter grief. But Liu Feng and Meng Da both flicked their sleeves and went inside. Knowing the matter had failed, Liao Hua reflected that he must report to the King of Hanzhong and seek aid. He mounted his horse, rode out of the city hurling curses, and set off toward Chengdu.

p.src: Meanwhile, Lord Guan waited in Maicheng for the troops from Shangyong, but there was no sign of them. He had only five or six hundred men under him, more than half of them wounded. There was no grain in the city, and their suffering was severe. Suddenly it was reported that a man below the walls was calling upon them not to shoot, saying that he had words for the lord. Lord Guan ordered that he be admitted and questioned him; it was Zhuge Jin. Only this lone city remains, with neither provisions within nor reinforcements without; disaster may come at any moment. Why not heed my words, submit to the Marquis of Wu, and resume your command over Jingzhou and Xiangyang? Thus you may preserve your whole family. I pray you consider it carefully, my lord.” Lord Guan answered sternly, “I am but a common warrior from Jieliang, yet my lord has treated me as his own brother. How could I betray righteousness and surrender to an enemy state? If the city falls, there is only death. Say no more; leave the city at once. I mean to fight Sun Quan to the death!” Zhuge Jin said, “The Marquis of Wu wishes to form a marriage alliance with you, join forces to defeat Cao Cao, and together uphold the House of Han. He has no other intention. Why are you so obstinately deluded, my lord?”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, Guan Ping drew his sword and stepped forward, intending to behead Zhuge Jin. Returning to the Marquis of Wu, he said, “Lord Guan’s heart is iron and stone; he cannot be persuaded.” Sun Quan said, “He is a true loyal minister! What are we to do with a man like this?” Lü Fan said, “Allow me to divine whether the outcome will be auspicious or ill.” Sun Quan at once ordered him to perform the divination. Lü Fan divided the yarrow stalks and formed the hexagram “The Army,” earth over water; moreover, the Black Tortoise governed the responding line, signifying that the enemy would flee far away. Sun Quan asked Lü Meng, “The hexagram says the enemy will flee far away. By what strategy will you capture him?” Lü Meng laughed and said, “The signs of the hexagram agree perfectly with my plan.
